facts.claim: Smartraveller (last updated Tuesday 18/08/2026): 'You can't register an overseas marriage in Australia. But in most cases, your marriage is legally recognised here. To be recognised, when you got married it must have been: valid under the law of the country where it happened; valid under Australian law if it had occurred in Australia.'

Smartraveller: 'Australia doesn't recognise overseas marriages where one or both of the people are: already married to someone else; not old enough to get married; too closely related; forced to get married.' Also: 'Talk to a lawyer to confirm your overseas marriage certificate is valid in Australia.'

Attorney-General's Department, 'Get married' page: 'An overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was a valid marriage in the overseas country and would have been a valid marriage here.' 'Overseas marriages cannot be registered in Australia.' Overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised celebrant.
facts.conflicts: Page shows 'last updated 1 September 2021' in body text but og:updated_time 2024-06-13; content reflects the 12 June 2024 amendments. Treat as current as at October 2026.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 88C(1): Part VA applies to every marriage solemnised in a foreign country where, under the local law, the marriage was, at the time it was solemnised, recognised as valid (with a separate rule for marriages before a diplomatic or consular officer of another foreign country).

Marriage Act 1961 s 88D(1), verbatim: 'Subject to this section, a marriage to which this Part applies shall be recognised in Australia as valid.' s 88D(2): such a marriage 'shall not be recognised as valid' if: (a) either party was, at the time of the marriage, a party to a marriage with some other person that was then recognised in Australia as valid; (b) where one of the parties was, at the time of the marriage, domiciled in Australia, either party was not of marriageable age within the meaning of Part II; (c) the parties are within a prohibited relationship within the meaning of section 23B; or (d) the consent of either party was not a real consent for a reason set out in s 23B(1)(d)(i), (ii) or (iii). Text matches on legislation.gov.au compilation No. 34 (28 March 2026) and AustLII.
facts.source: https://www.legislation.gov.au/C1961A00012/latest/text (Marriage Act 1961, compilation No. 34, 28 March 2026); section text also at https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ma196185/

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 88D(3) and (4): where neither party was domiciled in Australia, the marriage is not recognised while either party is under 16; and a foreign marriage is not recognised at any time while it is voidable under the local law.
facts.source: https://www.legislation.gov.au/C1961A00012/latest/text (Marriage Act 1961, compilation No. 34, 28 March 2026); section text also at https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ma196185/

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 23B(1)(d): consent is not a real consent because (i) it was obtained by duress or fraud; (ii) that party is mistaken as to the identity of the other party or as to the nature of the ceremony performed; or (iii) that party did not understand the nature and effect of the marriage ceremony.

NSW Government (NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, page modified 2026-10-21), 'What makes an overseas marriage not legally recognised in Australia?': one party was validly married to another person; one party was not of marriageable age in Australia; the parties are too closely related to marry; consent was not real because it was obtained by duress or fraud, they were mistaken as to the identity of the other person, they did not understand the nature of the ceremony, or they were mentally incapable of understanding the nature and effect of a marriage ceremony.

BDM Victoria (updated 16 October 2024): an overseas marriage 'will generally be recognised if: It's recognised under the law of the country where the marriage took place; Both parties are at least 18 years of age; Neither party is married to another person at the time of marriage.'
facts.conflicts: BDM Victoria's 'at least 18' is a plain-English simplification. s 88D(2)(b) applies the marriageable-age rule only where a party was domiciled in Australia, and s 88D(3) uses 16 where neither was. For Australian-domiciled couples the effect is the same; the article should cite the Act's wording, not the 18 shorthand, for non-domiciled partners.

facts.claim: NSW Government: 'Overseas marriages cannot be registered in Australia and you cannot be issued an Australian marriage certificate if you have been married overseas.' You'll need to have 'registered your marriage in the country where it took place' and 'evidence of the marriage, such as a marriage certificate and any other supporting documents.'

BDM Victoria: if you married overseas you need to 'Make sure your marriage is registered in that country' and 'Have evidence of the marriage, including official, commemorative or keepsake documents you got at the time of the ceremony.'

NSW Government: if an overseas marriage is not legally recognised in Australia you'll generally need to consider getting legal advice, provide a statutory declaration relating to the validity of the marriage, and 'have an official marriage ceremony in Australia, the same as if you were not already married.'

Comune di Bagno a Ripoli (Florence), marriage of foreign citizens: 'L'Ufficiale di Stato Civile, una volta celebrato il matrimonio, trascriverà l'atto sui registri di Stato Civile, e rilascerà il certificato / estratto di matrimonio' (once the marriage is celebrated, the civil registrar transcribes the act in the civil status registers and issues the marriage certificate or extract).

Comune di Gossolengo: a concordat (Catholic) marriage has civil effects 'a condizione che l'atto relativo sia trascritto nei registri dello stato civile' (on condition that the act is transcribed in the civil registers); the act signed by the couple and witnesses must be sent to the civil registrar within 5 days for transcription; civil effects run from the day of the ceremony.

Marriage Act 1961 s 88G(1): a document purporting to be the original or a certified copy of a certificate, entry or record of a marriage solemnised in a foreign country, issued by an authority of that country, 'is, for all purposes, prima facie evidence of the facts stated in the document and of the validity of the marriage to which the document relates' (unless proved the issuing authority was not competent, s 88G(2)).
facts.conflicts: A structured extraction of the legislation.gov.au compilation returned the wrong text under the 88G label (it returned s 88B wording). The AustLII section page was read in full and is the text used; check s 88G against compilation No. 34 before quoting verbatim.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Rome, 'Marriage in Italy' PDF: 'You may apply for a marriage certificate (certificato di matrimonio) shortly before the wedding ceremony and you should receive it immediately after the ceremony.' 'Ask to have an Apostille affixed to the Italian Marriage certificate by the Italian authorities at the Prefettura of the city where you get married, so that it may [be] legally valid once you return to Australia.' 'During the peak marriage season (May to September), it could be difficult to get an appointment for the marriage celebrant and to apply for the Apostille.'
facts.conflicts: The PDF has no visible issue date. Its wording ('so that it may legally valid') implies the apostille is needed for validity; under s 88D validity does not depend on the apostille. The article should say the apostille lets Australian agencies accept the certificate as a genuine Italian public document, not that it makes the marriage valid.

facts.claim: Prefettura di Udine (Italian Ministry of the Interior): the Apostille is the form of legalisation under the Hague Convention of 5 October 1961 for public documents to be used abroad; civil status certificates issued by comuni are apostilled by the Prefettura; 'l'apostille non ha scadenza' (the apostille does not expire), so a second one is not needed on the same document, though the underlying document may have its own validity period.
facts.conflicts: Read via structured extraction, not full text. Page metadata is noindex. Fine for 'the Prefettura apostilles comune certificates'; do not quote processing times.

facts.claim: Comune di Parma: multilingual civil status extracts (estratti plurilingue) are drawn up under the Vienna Convention of 8 September 1976 and are valid without translation or legalisation only among the Convention's countries. The listed countries are Austria, Belgium, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Cape Verde, Croatia, Estonia, France, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Luxembourg, North Macedonia, Moldova, Montenegro, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, Spain, Switzerland and Turkey. Australia is not listed. There are no multilingual extracts for civil unions.
facts.conflicts: Read via structured extraction. The 'valid without translation or legalisation' benefit applies only among Convention countries; because Australia is not listed, an Australian agency is not bound to accept the extract without translation. No Australian agency publishes whether it accepts an Italian multilingual extract.

facts.claim: EU e-Justice Portal and EUR-Lex summary of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191: the Regulation applies to public documents issued by one EU Member State that need to be presented to the authorities of another Member State. Its optional multilingual standard forms (including marriage) are translation aids attached to the public document, issued and signed by an authority of the issuing EU country, and not filled in by citizens.
facts.conflicts: EU official sources (not Italian or Australian government). They confirm the forms work between EU Member States only; nothing makes them binding on Australian agencies.

facts.claim: Australian Passport Office, 'Change of name or gender': 'If you change your family name because of a change in your marital status, you can choose to get a new passport or keep using your current one. We recommend booking travel in the name that's in your passport.' 'There are certain circumstances where we'll always need a name change certificate. This applies to any of the following: ... you were born in Australia and married or entered into a registered relationship overseas.'

Australian Passport Office: 'We'll accept foreign certificates only if you can't get an Australian equivalent because you were: born overseas; live overseas; married or entered into the relationship overseas. You must have become an Australian citizen before you entered the marriage or relationship. Foreign certificates must also be legalised. Any documents not in English need to be translated in full by an approved translation service.' Mandatory linking documents for a married name are an Australian birth or citizenship certificate plus a marriage certificate issued by an Australian RBDM, a registered relationship certificate, or an RBDM name change certificate.

Australian Passport Office, 'Interpreting and translation': 'If your documents aren't in English, you'll need to get them translated in full and stamped by an accredited translator before you show them to us.' In Australia, NAATI can help you find a translator; overseas, the nearest Australian embassy or consulate gives a list of approved translation services.

Services Australia, 'How to update your name with Centrelink' (page last updated 18 August 2026): for a marriage surname change it accepts 'an Australian marriage certificate for surname changes only' issued by Births, Deaths and Marriages; 'If you changed your name overseas, you'll need to provide us with original evidence from the Department of Home Affairs'; 'We don't accept ceremonial marriage certificates as a supporting document for a legal name change.'
facts.conflicts: Read via structured extraction. The page does not say whether an apostilled Italian certificate is accepted for an Australian-born citizen's surname change; the Home Affairs line appears aimed at people whose name changed before migrating. Medicare's requirements were not checked.

facts.claim: Department of Home Affairs, 'Popular questions': 'All documents not in English must be translated into English. Translators in Australia must be accredited by the National Accreditation Authority for Translators and Interpreters.' 'You must submit both the original document (non-English) and the translated document.' For translations made outside Australia, check the 'Gather your documents' section of the relevant visa or citizenship page.

Smartraveller: 'A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage. But you may be unable to use it as proof of a name change. Find out from your local registry of births, deaths and marriages.'

Attorney-General's Department: 'You may be able to use your overseas marriage certificate to prove that you got married. However, some states and territories don't accept overseas marriage certificates if you want to change your name.'

NSW Government (NSW Registry of BDM, modified 2026-10-21): 'If you were married overseas, your overseas marriage certificate cannot be used to change your surname after marriage. Note, even though your overseas marriage certificate cannot be used to change your name, this does not mean that your marriage is not recognised in Australia. Instead, you'll need to apply for an official change of name.'

BDM Victoria (updated 16 October 2024), 'Changing your family name': 'If you were born or married overseas, you can't take your spouse's family name automatically. You need to apply to change your name.'

Queensland Government (qld.gov.au, managed by BDM, modified 7 October 2026): 'If you married overseas, you may not be able to take your partner's family name automatically. This is because some organisations don't accept overseas documents as proof of identity. Some organisations may need an official change of name document.' You need to change your name at the Registry if you married overseas and previously changed your name with the Registry to your partner's name.

Western Australian Government, Registry of BDM 'Marriages' page (last modified 18 September 2026): 'If you were married overseas, you may be required to register a formal change of name with the Registry before your married surname is accepted by some organisations.' 'It is recommended that you check with the relevant authority to determine their specific requirements.'

South Australia (SA.GOV.AU 'Register a change of name', modified 10 September 2026): no registration is needed to take a partner's surname after marrying in Australia; 'If you were married overseas and want to take on your partner's surname, you should contact the relevant authority or business, such as your bank or the Australian Passport Office to see what evidence you need to give them.'

Tasmania, Births, Deaths and Marriages 'Register a change of name' (updated 12 November 2025): you do not need to register a new name if you marry in Australia and take your partner's surname; 'If you were married overseas and want to take on your partner's surname, you should contact the relevant authority or business, such as your bank or the Australian Passport Office to see what evidence you need to give them.'

ACT, Access Canberra 'Change your name as an adult' (modified 20 April 2026), 'Marriage overseas': 'If you want to change your name after marriage overseas, you may experience difficulties in using your foreign marriage certificate to support the change. You may be asked to register a change of name.' Separate processes apply if you were born in the ACT or outside it.

Northern Territory, NT.GOV.AU 'Legally change your name' (dated 31 August 2022): the page lists a marriage certificate as a supporting document when changing a name after marriage, but publishes no rule on using an overseas marriage certificate to take a spouse's surname. NT rule: not published.

Attorney-General's Department, 'Get married': give the Notice of Intended Marriage to the authorised celebrant 'at least 1 month' and 'no more than 18 months' before the wedding; 'If there is less than 1 month until your wedding, talk to your authorised marriage celebrant. You may be able to get married if a prescribed authority approves it.' 'Your authorised marriage celebrant will also need to meet separately and in person with each party to a marriage' (changes from 12 June 2024).

Marriage Act 1961 s 113(1), verbatim: 'Except in accordance with this section: (a) persons who are already legally married to each other shall not, in Australia or under Part V, go through a form or ceremony of marriage with each other; and (b) a person who is authorised by this Act to solemnise marriages shall not purport to solemnise a marriage in Australia or under Part V between persons who inform the first-mentioned person that they are already legally married to each other or whom the first-mentioned person knows or has reason to believe to be already legally married to each other.'
facts.source: https://www.legislation.gov.au/C1961A00012/latest/text (Marriage Act 1961, compilation No. 34, 28 March 2026); section text also at https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ma196185/

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 113(2) and (3): where there is a doubt whether the couple are legally married, whether an overseas marriage would be recognised as valid by an Australian court, or whether it could be proved in legal proceedings, they may marry again in Australia 'as if they had not previously gone through a form or ceremony of marriage'; they give the celebrant a statutory declaration of the earlier ceremony (date, place, circumstances) with a barrister's or solicitor's certificate endorsed on it that there is such a doubt.
facts.source: https://www.legislation.gov.au/C1961A00012/latest/text (Marriage Act 1961, compilation No. 34, 28 March 2026); section text also at https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ma196185/

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 113(5) and (6): nothing prevents a couple already legally married to each other from going through a religious ceremony of marriage in Australia if they produce a certificate of their existing marriage and sign a witnessed statement that they previously married each other, are the parties named in the certificate and have no reason to believe the overseas marriage would not be recognised; the person performing it must not issue any certificate of marriage under the Act.
facts.source: https://www.legislation.gov.au/C1961A00012/latest/text (Marriage Act 1961, compilation No. 34, 28 March 2026); section text also at https://www.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/viewdoc/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ma196185/

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department, 'Marriage equality in Australia': 'If we recognise your marriage, you can't get married again in Australia. But you may choose to hold another type of ceremony, such as: confirmation of vows, recommitment ceremony.'

Attorney-General's Department, 'Marriage equality in Australia' (og:updated 3 December 2025): 'Since 9 December 2017, same-sex marriages that took place overseas are generally recognised in Australia.' The Marriage Act defines marriage as 'the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life'. Same-sex married couples are treated the same as other married couples whether the marriage happened before or after 9 December 2017 or overseas (if it would be recognised as a valid overseas marriage).
BDM Victoria: 'Recognised marriages include overseas same-sex marriages that occurred prior to December 2017.'

Comune di Firenze, 'Unioni civili, Legge 20 maggio 2016 n. 76 (Legge Cirinnà)': 'L'unione civile è l'istituto giuridico finalizzato a costituire rapporti civili tra persone dello stesso sesso' (the civil union is the legal institution for same-sex couples). Two adults of the same sex form it by declaration before the civil registrar in the presence of two witnesses; a foreign citizen presents a nulla osta from their country's competent authority or a certificate showing free status; the parties may choose a common surname from their surnames by declaration to the registrar.

Italian Ministry of Justice, 'Coppie di nazionalità diverse: Matrimonio': 'Il matrimonio contratto all'estero da cittadini italiani con persona dello stesso sesso produce gli effetti dell'unione civile regolata dalla legge italiana' (a same-sex marriage contracted abroad by Italian citizens produces the effects of an Italian civil union). Confirms Italian law treats same-sex unions as civil unions, not marriages.
facts.conflicts: Search-result text only; page not opened in full. Context only, not for quoting. The article's Italy claim (civil union, not marriage) rests on fact_42.

facts.claim: State relationship laws (Tasmania Relationships Act 2003; Queensland Civil Partnerships Act 2011) let a regulation treat a relationship 'registered under a corresponding law' as a registered relationship locally. No Australian government source was found that prescribes an Italian unione civile or says how Australia treats one.
facts.conflicts: Search-result text only. Whether any state prescribes Italy is unconfirmed, and the AGD, Smartraveller, NSW and Victorian pages are silent on overseas civil unions. Keep [[VERIFY]].

facts.claim: Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, 'How do I apply for divorce?': 'Parties to a divorce that were married overseas can apply for a divorce in Australia as long as one of the parties to the divorce meets the eligibility criteria and the marriage was solemnised overseas according to the law of that country and a marriage certificate was produced.' Eligibility: one party is an Australian citizen by birth, descent or grant, or is lawfully present and intends to keep living in Australia and has lived here for at least the last 12 months; the parties must have been separated for 12 months and 1 day or longer. A marriage certificate not in English must be translated and attached, with the original, to an Affidavit of Translation of Marriage Certificate from the translator (NAATI has a directory).
Smartraveller: 'Marrying an Australian citizen doesn't ensure you can come to Australia. Or become a citizen. Foreign citizens must follow Australia's immigration laws to enter and live here.'

insider_details.detail: Put the apostille in the plan, not in the honeymoon. The Rome embassy advises getting it at the Prefettura of the city where you marry, and warns that appointments are hard to get from May to September. Book it for the first working days after the wedding and before anyone flies home. An apostille does not expire, so one is enough.

For use in Australia, ask the comune for the full marriage certificate, have it apostilled, and get a full English translation. The multilingual extract is free and quick, but its no-translation benefit only applies among Vienna Convention countries and Australia is not one. The EU multilingual forms only work between EU Member States. The Passport Office and Home Affairs both ask for full translations of non-English documents.

If either of you was born in Australia and plans to take the other's surname, the Passport Office will always want an Australian registry change of name certificate, whatever the Italian certificate says. Book honeymoon and return flights in the name on your current passport, and apply to your state registry after you get home.

A Catholic church wedding in Italy is only legally a marriage once the parish sends the act to the comune and the comune transcribes it, which should happen within 5 days. Before you leave, ask for the comune's certificate, not the parish's. That is the document the apostille and every Australian agency will expect.

For a second celebration at home after a legal Italian wedding, brief your celebrant that you are already married. Under s 113 they cannot solemnise a marriage between you. What you can have is a confirmation of vows or recommitment ceremony, or a religious ceremony under s 113(5) once you show your existing certificate, and no Australian marriage certificate is issued for it. Remarrying under s 113(2) is only for genuine doubt about the Italian marriage, and needs a lawyer's certificate.

Same-sex couples can only enter a civil union in Italy, not a marriage, and no Australian government source says how a civil union is treated here. The clear route is to marry legally in Australia first and hold the Italian day as a celebration. Lodge the Notice of Intended Marriage at least 1 month (and no more than 18 months) ahead, and allow for the celebrant to meet each of you separately and in person.

agency_proof_table.what_official_sources_say: A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage. Under s 88G, a certificate from the competent Italian authority is prima facie evidence of the marriage and its validity.

If you were born in Australia and married overseas, you always need an Australian RBDM name change certificate. Foreign certificates must be legalised, and non-English documents translated in full by an approved or accredited translator. You can keep your current passport after a marriage name change; book travel in your passport name.

For surname changes it lists an Australian marriage certificate; for a name changed overseas it asks for original Home Affairs evidence; ceremonial certificates are not accepted. Its position on an apostilled Italian certificate is not published.

agency_proof_table.what_official_sources_say: SA and Tasmania registries tell couples married overseas to ask the bank or Passport Office what evidence they need. QLD, WA and ACT say some organisations may need an official change of name document. No bank policy is published here.

Documents not in English must be translated into English; translators in Australia must be NAATI-accredited; submit the original and the translation. Marriage does not by itself give a right to live in Australia.
Couples married overseas can apply in Australia if one party meets the eligibility criteria; a non-English certificate is filed with a translator's affidavit.

state_surname_rules.rule: An overseas marriage certificate cannot be used to change your surname; apply for an official change of name. This does not mean the marriage is not recognised.

You may not be able to take your partner's name automatically; some organisations need an official change of name document.
You may be required to register a formal change of name before some organisations accept your married surname.
Contact the relevant authority or business (for example your bank or the Passport Office) to see what evidence they need.

You may have difficulties using a foreign marriage certificate and may be asked to register a change of name.
For a passport in the new surname, the Passport Office always needs an Australian RBDM name change certificate.
